claims.text: As-synthesized high-entropy nanoalloys can be prepared as single-phase, approximately random solid solutions at nanometer scale.
Minor dopant additions or compositional ratio adjustments can promote short-range or local chemical ordering in high-entropy nanoalloys.
High-temperature short-range ordering and chemical clustering can occur in compositionally varied Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloys.
Locally ordered regions act as kinetic barriers to atomic motion.
Increasing local chemical order reduces atomistic diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Diffusion drives phase segregation in high-entropy nanoalloys during heating.
Diffusion drives surface reconstruction in high-entropy nanoparticles during heating.
The structural stability of high-entropy alloys reflects an interplay involving configurational entropy and constituent-element mixing enthalpies.
Composition changes and annealing temperature can cause high-entropy solid solutions to decompose into multiple phases.
Induced local ordering will delay the onset of phase decomposition relative to a random-solid-solution baseline.
Induced local ordering will reduce elemental segregation relative to the baseline.
Induced local ordering will improve retention of a single-phase structure during high-temperature annealing.
Atomic diffusion is activated over the proposed 800–1200 °C testing range.
The stabilization mechanism is limited to nanoparticle sizes for which nanoscale effects are dominant.

contradictions.description: The intervention is defined as dopant additions or ratio changes, but the baseline is said to have an identical overall composition; the experimental design then relaxes this to only similar compositions. A compositionally modified sample cannot simultaneously have an identical overall composition, and composition differences would confound the effect of local ordering.
